Connectome · Dynamics · Topology

The fly's compass is a ring. Is its activity one too?

A fruit fly knows which way it faces with a ring of neurons in its brain. On the left that circuit is running live, wired with real synapse counts from the fly connectome. Turn the fly, watch the bump of activity follow, then use persistent homology to ask whether the activity itself lies on a ring.

1

A ring in the brain

椭球体

In the middle of the fly brain is a doughnut-shaped structure, the ellipsoid body. About 46 E-PG neurons (47 in the FlyWire brain) tile it in 16 wedges. At any moment a single bump of activity sits somewhere on the ring, and when the fly turns, the bump turns with it, even in complete darkness. The fly is integrating its own angular velocity, like a sailor doing dead reckoning.

That is what the ring on the left shows. Each wedge's orange is the mean firing of the E-PG neurons in it. The strip underneath is the protocerebral bridge, where the same neurons hand the bump to P-EN cells, which shift it left or right as the fly turns.

Try it. Switch Auto-turn off and drag the fly a quarter turn. The error should stay small. Leave it in darkness for a minute and the decoded heading slowly drifts, as a real fly's does; turn the landmark on and it snaps back.
2

Wired from the connectome

连接组

Nobody hand-designed this network. The 152 neurons and their 129,473 synapses come from the hemibrain, an electron-microscopy reconstruction of a female fly's brain. Each neuron's input is the sum of its partners' activity weighted by how many synapses connect them.

Two brains. Switch Brain to FlyWire to rewire the same model from a second, independently reconstructed fly: a whole female brain imaged and proofread by a different team with different software. FlyWire does not label the bridge glomeruli, so each E-PG neuron's place on the ring was inferred from its wiring alone (neurons in the same wedge share partners); on the hemibrain, where the answer is known, that inference is off by 7° on average, less than half a wedge. Fitted the same way, the FlyWire circuit also forms a bump that follows the fly. Over 20 s in the dark it drifts about as much as the hemibrain circuit (28° average error against 29°), though it is less precise over the first few seconds (18° against 12°).

Only 49 numbers were fitted, never the synapse counts: one gain for each pair of cell types, a bias and a time constant per type, and one gain on the angular-velocity input. The model has six cell types, so that is 36 + 6 + 6 + 1 = 49. With raw synapse counts and a single overall gain, no stable bump forms.

The six cell types. E-PG carry the bump from ring to bridge; P-EN1 and P-EN2 shift it when the fly turns; P-EG carry it back to the ring; Δ7 spread inhibition across the bridge; and E-PGt are four E-PG-like neurons that innervate the outermost bridge glomeruli. E-PGt have their own gains in the fit, but the matrix below draws them in the E-PG block.

Connection matrix 152 × 152 · hemibrain

Rows receive, columns send, sorted by cell type and bridge glomerulus. Red excites, blue inhibits. The diagonal stripes are the ring: each wedge talks most to its neighbours. The matrix follows the circuit you pick on the left.

3

The shape of activity

状态空间

At each moment, the E-PG firing rates are one point in a space with one axis per neuron: 46 dimensions. As the fly turns, that point moves. If the circuit really is a compass, the point can only go round: the cloud of all moments should form a closed loop, one point on the loop per heading.

State space 0 s recorded

true heading 0°→360°projected onto the top 2 principal components

A loop in a picture is suggestive, but a projection can create or hide loops. Topology lets us ask the question in all 46 dimensions at once.

4

Birth and death of a loop

生与死

Pick a distance ε. Join every two recorded moments that are closer than ε, and fill in every triangle whose three sides are all joined. Now grow ε from zero. At first there are only scattered points. Then neighbours join into one ring, and a hole appears: a loop is born. Grow ε further and edges start to cross the ring, the triangles fill the hole, and the loop dies.

Persistent homology records every loop's birth and death. Plot each loop as a point at (birth, death) and you get the persistence diagram found in the papers. Noise makes loops that die almost as soon as they are born, close to the diagonal. A real ring makes one point far above it.

Let the fly turn all the way round (or fast-forward), then compute.

Filtration Ripser · WebAssembly

The 400 analysed moments, with a line between any two closer than ε in the full 46-D space.

How do we know a loop is not chance? The shuffle test slides each neuron's time series by a random offset. Every neuron keeps its own firing statistics, but the coordination between neurons is destroyed. The longest loop any shuffle produces sets the grey band. A loop that rises above the band is real. With 20 shuffles, a recording with no structure would beat all of them with probability 1/21, so clearing the band is a test at roughly the 5% level.

5

Break the circuit

破坏

If the ring in the activity comes from the wiring, then breaking the wiring should break the ring. Each experiment below runs a fresh copy of the selected brain's circuit for 60 s of a fly wandering in the dark, then computes the persistence diagram and a 20-shuffle test, exactly as above. All four diagrams share one scale.

runs the hemibrain circuit · about 25 s
Why Δ7 matters. Δ7 neurons spread inhibition across the whole bridge. Without them, excitation runs away and every wedge saturates: the state collapses to a single point and the loop has nothing to go round. With the wiring shuffled within each pair of cell types, the cell-type totals are kept but the neighbour structure is lost, and so is the ring.
6

A real mouse, awake and asleep

真实的小鼠

Everything so far is a model. Here is a recording. A mouse brain has no ring-shaped structure, but its head-direction cells fire when the animal faces one particular direction. These are 80 of them, recorded together in the postsubiculum while the mouse explored an arena and later slept.

Mouse State

Replay 60 s · real spikes

Each dot is one cell, placed at the direction it prefers; brightness is how fast it is firing. Orange line: the direction read out from the cells; blue: where the mouse's head actually points.

The same population as points in state space (top two components), coloured by the head direction at that moment.

Persistence diagrams awake vs REM sleep

The ring survives sleep. In REM sleep the eyes are closed and the head is still, yet the bump keeps travelling around the same loop, as Chaudhuri et al. (2019) found. The fly model's ring came from wiring; the mouse's ring is also internal: it is a property of the network, not of what the animal sees.

How the mouse data were processed. 100 ms bins, square root, 200 ms smoothing; each moment divided by the total population activity (otherwise the overall firing level dominates); z-scored; top 6 principal components; the 80% most active moments, then the densest half; 400 points evenly spaced in time. The grey band comes from 50 surrogates that circularly shift each cell's spike train, sent through the identical pipeline; it is the longest loop any of them produces, so clearing it is a test at about the 2% level (1/51). These diagrams were computed offline with Ripser; the analysis code is in the repository.

What this shows, and what it doesn't

The anatomy and the activity have the same shape. A ring of neurons, wired as the connectome says with only cell-type-level tuning, produces activity whose high-dimensional state space is a single persistent loop. Breaking the wiring removes the loop.

This is a simulation constrained by the connectome, not a recording from a fly. Neurotransmitter signs (E-PG, P-EN, P-EG excitatory; Δ7 inhibitory) are standard assumptions. A long H1 bar shows that the states form a loop; it does not by itself prove a ring attractor, which also needs the bump to persist and move continuously. Real recordings of mouse head-direction cells show the same topology, awake and asleep (chapter 6).
